epic.name: The shared expense request list
unverifiedAssumptions: Verify that requests from a cancelled file never appear in this list: the app marks possible duplicates by comparing every request the service returns (minus the rejected ones), on the understanding that a cancelled file's requests are never sent at all. If the service does return them, you will see requests marked as possible duplicates that should not have been compared.

Verify that transaction dates all come back written the same way (e.g. `2026-04-15 15:00:00`): the app orders by date, matches possible duplicates on date, and now also compares dates against an earliest/latest range using the way the service writes them. If the same date can arrive written differently — or with a time of day on some rows and not others — ordering can look wrong, two genuine duplicates may be missed, and a date range can leave out requests that really do fall inside it. A request dated on the last day of your range is the one most likely to go missing.

Verify how many requests come back in one go: the service sends every imported request in a single response with no paging, and this screen is built for up to ten thousand. If your live data is much larger, the first load will be slow or may not finish — and no test would show that.

Check the Type column against your live data: the app spells out 'Credit — money in' and 'Debit — money out' for the codes C and D, which is what the sample file uses. The service's own documentation spells 'Debit' out in full instead, and anything the app has no wording for is shown exactly as the service sent it (deliberately, not a bug). If your Type column shows raw values, that is which convention your service uses.

Confirm the request-list link now reads 'Expense requests' in the header for both people, and that a Finance Uploader seeing that link (they could not before) is what you want — they can read every request but are offered nothing to decide.

Confirm what should happen when a signed-out person types an address that does not exist: they are now sent to the sign-in screen rather than shown a 'page not found'. Signed in, a mistyped address shows 'not found' with the app header still on it, so there is a way out.

Search treats what you type as plain text, ignoring capitals, and matches the amount exactly as the table prints it — so searching 15750 finds the R15,750 request but searching '15,750' or 'R15750' does not. If finance staff expect to search formatted amounts, that needs saying.

If the service ever returned a request with a blank status, file name or transaction type, that blank is not offered as a filter choice (there would be nothing to name it with, and the picker cannot hold an empty choice). The sample data has no blanks, so this has never been exercised against the real service.

The amount range compares the plain number and ignores which currency a request is in. Every request carries a Currency and the sample data is all ZAR, so if your live data ever mixes currencies, a range of 100 to 200 will match amounts between 100 and 200 in any of them. Confirm that is what finance staff expect.

An amount bound is typed as a plain number — no currency symbol, no thousands separator (the field accepts digits, a decimal point and a minus sign only, to the cent). If people expect to type 'R1 500' or '1,500', that needs saying.

A date bound is entered as a calendar date and matched on the DAY, so the time of day recorded against a request is deliberately ignored at both ends of the range. Confirm nobody needs to narrow to part of a day.

R13 says a column sorts ascending on the first activation and descending on the second, but not what a third does. Clicking the same heading a third time returns it to ascending (so the two directions keep cycling) rather than clearing the ordering — please confirm that is the behaviour you expect.

Sorting the Account number column orders by the four digits shown on screen, not by the full account number, because ordering rows by a value POPIA does not let us display would leak the order of those hidden values. For the same reason the Type column sorts by the wording you read ('Credit — money in') rather than the backend's raw code ('C'). Please confirm both readings.

At phone width a request's card shows its reference, status, amount and transaction date, and NOT its account number — the reader gets that (masked, with the reveal) by opening the request. R16 asks for the identifier plus 'two-to-three key values', so which three was this story's choice; confirm those are the three you want on a phone.

The detail panel prints LastChangedDate and TransactionDate exactly as the service sends them (e.g. '2026-04-16 11:05:00') rather than in a friendlier local format — deliberate, because this epic does not normalise dates and the format is already carried as an unverified assumption. Worth confirming the raw form is acceptable on a screen a person reads.

An already-approved request still counts in the duplicate comparison — only rejected requests are excluded (BR3 names exactly two exclusions: cancelled files and rejected requests). So a newly imported request that matches one already approved IS marked. Confirm that is what you want; the alternative reading of 'two imported requests' would compare only requests still awaiting a decision.
The Approver's duplicate notification stays on screen until it is dismissed, unlike the app's other notifications, which fade after about five seconds. Confirm that is welcome rather than intrusive.
